title: Chapter 154 – The Falling Line
html:
[The Silver Road – Lin Yue]

Yue has been deaf for thirteen years, and she has never once been lonely on the road.

That surprises her. She had expected the silence to isolate her, to put a pane of glass between her and the world, and for the first year it did. The kitchen was a room of moving mouths. The school was a flock of silent birds. But the road is different. The road is a single long note, running under her feet from horizon to horizon, and she walks along it as a swimmer rides a current, and everything that is not the road falls away.

She is aware, in a remote, contented sort of way, that she is happy.

It is the fifth morning. The silver line runs north across a high wide plain of yellow grass, and the frost has gone from the ground, and the wind is mild. Ahead of her Pebble trots with his tail up, his cracked back gleaming faintly in the sun. Behind her Bell is complaining silently, with the elaborate gestures of a woman whose boots have blisters. And at the rear, walking with his staff and his white head bare, her brother is talking to himself again.

He does it often now. She watches his lips move. He does not mutter; he speaks in a clear, low, courteous murmur, with pauses, as one converses with a friend across a table. Sometimes he smiles. Sometimes he stops in the road for a moment with his head bent, listening. It is not madness. She knows what it is. She has seen it in the way a mother looks at a child sleeping in her arms.

He's telling the boy about the sky, says Pebble, who has dropped back to walk beside her. His voice, as always, comes inside her head, deep and dry, like the sound of a bell heard through a wall. They've been at it since dawn. The boy wants to know why it's blue.

What did Jian say?

That he doesn't know. A pause. The boy said that was fine. They'd find out together.

She laughs, silently. Pebble's black eyes crinkle. They walk on.

* * *

She hears the village before she sees it.

It is not a sound. It is a texture, a roughness in the road's long note, like a thread snagged on a splinter. She stops, and Bell nearly walks into her. Far ahead, where the yellow plain dips into a shallow valley, there is something that hums differently from the grass and the wind. It is small and warm and busy and slightly out of tune, and it has the unmistakable tone of many people living close together.

Smoke, signs Bell, pointing.

A thin gray column rises from the valley. As they come over the lip of the ridge, the village opens beneath them, a scatter of round felt tents on a sheltered slope above a frozen stream. There are perhaps forty. Sheep pens made of wattle. A dozen horses tethered by a rail. Children running between the tents. A line of washing, bright red and blue.

And in the middle of it all, standing at the end of the silver road as if she had been waiting there all morning, a woman in a quilted felt cloak is staring up the hill with her hands over her mouth.

She has seen your brother, says Pebble.

How can she tell?

Look at her face.

Yue looks. The woman is perhaps sixty. She is broad and brown and weathered, with a thick white braid down her back and a face like a good loaf. As Jian reaches the edge of the village she begins to walk, and then to run, awkwardly, with her skirts bunched in her fists, and she cannot stop. She hits him in the chest with the full force of a woman who has driven oxen all her life and throws both arms around his neck.

"Teacher," she says. She is crying. Yue can read it on her lips. "Teacher, teacher. You are so old."

* * *

His name was Temur. He was nine years old when Jian first rode into the valley of the Odgerel and found a boy of the tribe sitting on a rock, drawing numbers in the mud with a stick. He had never been taught his letters. He had taught himself the shapes of the numbers from watching traders count, and had no way of knowing what they meant.

He is fifty-eight now. He is headman of the Four Streams. He has eleven grandchildren, a bad hip, and a slate that he wears on a cord around his neck.

She learns this in pieces, over the course of an afternoon, in a long smoky felt tent that smells of mutton fat and tea. The whole village has crowded in to look at the Teacher. They sit cross-legged on the carpets in rows, big-eyed children in front and old men behind, and watch Jian with the intense collective hush of an audience at a play. Bell is explaining what a doctor does to a circle of delighted old women. Yue sits in the corner with a bowl of salt tea on her knee and watches faces.

It is the best way to follow a conversation. People who speak with their mouths lie only with the corners. Temur does not lie at all. He leans toward Jian over the low table, huge and grave in his felt cloak, and tells him everything in the order it happened.

"After you left," he says, "I kept the slate. I taught the others. We have a school now. Forty children. Eleven of them can read." He pauses. "My father died eleven winters ago. In his sleep, in the spring. He asked for you."

"I'm sorry."

"No." Temur shakes his head. "He said, tell the Teacher the sheep are fine. That is all. It was a very good death."

Jian laughs, a short astonished sound, and wipes his eyes. The boy in the room is laughing too; Yue can see it in the way her brother's shoulders shake. She lets the tea warm her hands. She feels the rich, dense, human hum of the tent, a hundred small notes weaving, and under it, rising from the soil beneath the carpets, a faint low drone that she has been trying to ignore for an hour.

She looks at Pebble. He is sitting by her knee with his head cocked.

You hear it, he says.

Yes.

It's the same one. From the road. It's louder here.

What is it?

I think, says Pebble slowly, that we should ask the headman about the grass.

* * *

Bell is called away before the dumplings are cold.

A child has fallen from a pony. It is a boy of seven, all elbows and scabs, and he lies on a felt mat in the next tent with his leg bent at an angle that makes the women go quiet and the men look at the floor. Yue follows because she follows everything that moves. She stands in the doorway and watches her niece kneel down in the lamp-light, take the small foot in both hands, and say something low and level that makes the child stop screaming.

She does not hear what. She does not need to. She watches the hands. Bell has her grandmother's hands, small and broad and sure, and she works like a woman threading a needle: two fingers to find the ends of the bone, a slow steady pull, the leg straightening as if by agreement, the boy's mouth opening on a gasp and then going slack with surprise. Splints. Wool. A strip of clean linen. A pill from her satchel, which she crushes in honey and puts on the child's tongue.

"He will walk in six weeks," Bell says, to the circle of faces. Yue reads it off her lips. "He must not ride for ten. Tell his mother that."

They tell her. The mother, a stout young woman with a baby at her breast, takes Bell's hand and presses it to her forehead and says something Yue can't catch. Bell goes red to the ears.

"It's nothing," she says, awkwardly. "It's a clean break."

It is not nothing, Yue signs, from the doorway.

Bell sees her and grins. It is her mother's grin, lopsided and quick. You are not supposed to be watching.

I'm very proud.

Stop it. But she is blushing again, and she bends her head over the splint to hide it.

* * *

She watches Temur's face change as he answers.

"The grass," he says. He lays down his cup. "Yes. You have a good eye, Teacher. It is why I called the elders." His voice drops. His hand goes to the slate on his chest. "Come outside. I should like to show you."

They go out, all five of them, into the cold bright afternoon. The sun is lowering. Long gold light lies across the valley, and the tents cast blue shadows on the frost. Temur leads them up a path behind the village to a rise, and from the top of it the whole steppe opens to the north.

It is yellow grass as far as the eye can see. Mile after mile of it, rolling, endless, silver-edged in the sun. But it is wrong. She sees it before the others. Her whole body knows it. The grass is flat. In long straight bands, wide as a road, running north and south as far as she can see, it has been trampled to the ground and left there, a dead pale yellow, like a field after a harvest.

"The herds," says Temur quietly. "Not ours. We have eleven hundred sheep. These are the wild ones. The long-horn. The wild asses. The great deer of the north." He swallows. "They came through in the autumn. It took them eleven days. Ten thousand head, perhaps more. They did not stop for water. They did not stop to eat. They ran south, all of them, as if the sky were on fire."

"South," says Jian.

"Toward your Garden. Toward the river." Temur lifts his slate and shows them: a column of tally marks, scratched with a nail, each a day. "And then it began again. In the winter. Not herds. Hunters. Wolves. The black bears. Things I have no name for. They went through at night." His voice shakes. "My eldest son counted forty horned wolves in a single hour. They did not look at us. They did not even smell the horses."

Yue stands very still. A cold wind moves her cloak. In the clean ruled stripes of trampled grass, she can hear, now, the long fading echo of ten thousand feet. It lies on the steppe like a scar.

"What is behind them?" says Jian.

"I do not know." Temur turns his big weathered face toward the northern horizon. "No one comes back from the Wall. But my grandmother told me once, when I was small, that the grass-people have a word for this. A very old word. Tide."

"Tide?"

"The Long Tide. It comes when the mountain is full." He shivers. "She said that the last one was six hundred years ago. That the tents were swept away. That the sky was black with the wings of things that had no names. She said that the grass remembers."

Nobody speaks. The sun touches the rim of the hills. And in the long gold silence, Yue feels it under her feet, faint and enormous, a single slow thud.

Knock.

* * *

They stay the night in Temur's tent, because he will not hear of anything else.

It is a long loud supper. There is mutton and dumplings and sour milk and a fiery clear drink that Bell sips once and refuses to describe. There are songs. There are many songs. A very old man with a horsehair fiddle plays something slow and wild that makes the children go quiet, and Temur's granddaughter, a fierce small girl of nine, reads aloud from a slate, in a high careful voice, a letter Jian wrote forty-eight years ago. It is not a very good letter. It is mostly about the weather. She reads it as if it were scripture.

Yue sits at the edge of the firelight. She cannot hear the fiddle. But the felt floor under her thrums with it, and the fire's heat carries a rhythm of its own, and across the tent Jian is laughing at something the old man said, the real laugh, the young one, with his head thrown back. She hears it in the way the air hums around him.

He's happy, says Pebble.

Yes.

He doesn't get to be, very often. I think it surprises him.

I think it does.

Yue. The creature's voice is hesitant. I want to tell you something, and I do not know how.

Try.

The road is changing. He looks at her with his black unblinking eyes. It is not a mistake. It was always going to. But I did not tell your brother, because he was already carrying so much.

Changing how?

It does not go where we thought. The little paw rests on her knee. I remember the bronze door. I remember it at the foot of a cliff in the cold. I assumed it was beyond the Wall. On the far side, in the north. A pause. I think I was wrong. I think the road is not leading us past the mountains.

Then where?

Into them.

Her hands go still.

The Sky Wall is not a barrier, says Pebble. It is a house. It has been a house for six hundred years. And the door is in the front of it.

* * *

After the supper is done and the children have been put to bed under heaps of sheepskin, Yue goes to sit beside her brother at the edge of the fire.

He is alone. He has drawn a little apart, with his back against a saddle and his white head bowed, and the coals paint the lines of his face in red. He looks up as she settles beside him. She raises her eyebrows, and signs, with deliberate slowness, so that he cannot mistake it.

I'd like to meet him.

His face goes very still.

The boy, she adds. Properly. I've heard him once, through the Gate, asking if he was all right. I've felt him in the hum of you for thirteen years and I didn't know what it was. I'd like to say hello.

"Yue," he says aloud, and stops. She can read the hesitation in his mouth. He is afraid. She has seen that expression on him only a handful of times. It is the look of a man holding a very full cup.

Please.

He nods. He closes his eyes.

And she feels it. A change in the air, as when a candle is carried into a dark room. The lines of his face loosen. The set of his shoulders, which has been hard and old and braced for as long as she has known him, relaxes, and his head tilts a little on one side. When he opens his eyes they are the same eyes, gray and tired and shadowed. But they are looking at her in a way she has never seen. Shyly. Hopefully. Straight up, from a long way below.

Pebble, on her knee, clears his throat. He says hello, Aunt Yue.

She stares.

He says he's very sorry. He doesn't have the right words. He's never spoken to anyone but Jian and Mother and Father. The deep voice is gentle. He says he has been listening to you ring the bell for thirteen years. He says it is the most beautiful sound he knows.

She cannot see. Her eyes have filled. She puts out a hand and lays it on her brother's cheek, rough and lined and white-bristled, and she says aloud, in the slow thick voice of a woman who has not used it in years, "Hello, little one."

Jian's mouth, the boy's mouth, trembles.

He wants to know, says Pebble, whether you will teach him to sign.

She laughs, helplessly, through the tears. Of course. It's very easy. It's mostly rude.

He says he likes rude.

Everyone does. She wipes her face. Come here. Look at my hands. This one means hello.

And in the red light of the fire, with the steppe dark and enormous around them and the wind hissing in the grass, an old woman sits cross-legged on a felt carpet and teaches her brother's other self to sign, one word at a time, laughing and weeping, until the coals go gray.

* * *

She cannot sleep.

She lies in her blanket on the felt carpet with the heat of the stove on her face and the slow breathing of eleven strangers around her, and thinks about the Wall. It is a long dull ache of a thought. She has been hearing it for years, as a pressure on the edge of her mind, a faint thickness in the north. She had put it down to age.

She gets up, in the end, and goes out into the cold.

The camp is dark. The fire has burned to red. Overhead the stars burn white and enormous in a sky so clear that she can see the dust between them, and the silver road runs away beneath her feet like a river of milk. She walks to the end of the village and stands on the rise where Temur showed them the trampled grass. The wind is bitter. Her nose runs. She does not care.

She closes her eyes and listens.

It comes to her slowly. First the road: that long clean note. Under it, the sleeping village, the horses, the dogs. Under that, the soil of the steppe, a vast low thrum like a heartbeat. And under that, so far down that she can only feel it in her teeth, a sound she has known all her life and never once heard from here.

The Mother Tree.

It is singing.

Three hundred miles away, in a black winter orchard, a tree that is ninety years old and six hundred years old and perhaps ten thousand years old is singing, and the song comes up the silver road like water up a root. She cannot hear the words. There are no words. It is a single long rising phrase, over and over, a question asked in a language older than speech, and she has heard it before, once, on the night her brother flowered his Core.

Come home, it says, or come soon, or take care. She cannot tell. But it is not a warning. It is a mother calling a child in from the dusk.

She stands with her face lifted to the stars, and the tears run down her cheeks and freeze, and she does not wipe them away.

Yue.

It is Pebble. He has followed her out and sits on the rock at her feet, small and gray, with a pale line gleaming on his back.

I hear it too, he says.

What does it want?

I think it wants us to go on. He is quiet a moment. But there is something else under it. A second voice. Very faint. As if the tree were singing to someone who is not there.

Who?

I don't know. He looks north, where the black line of the mountains cuts the stars. But whoever he is, he is on the other side of that door. And he has been listening a very long time.

* * *

They leave at dawn, but not before Temur takes them to the grave.

It lies at the end of the village, on a low rise beyond the last tent, a heap of stones with a post at its head. On the post hangs a horse's tail dyed red, stiff with frost, and a string of small bronze bells that stir in the wind. Yue cannot hear them. She watches them tremble. Temur stands bareheaded beside the cairn, a huge shape in felt, and speaks to it for a while in his own tongue, low and easy, as a man speaks to a neighbor over a wall.

Then he stoops and picks up a stone. It is small and white and rounded. He places it, with great care, on the top of the heap, and steps back.

"He liked you," he says to Jian, in the common speech. "He was a hard man, my father. He said you were the first stranger who ever asked him a question and waited for the answer."

"I asked him about the sheep."

"Yes." Temur's smile is crooked. "He talked about it for a year."

Jian bends and, a little stiffly, lays a stone of his own. Beside him the boy is silent. Yue, watching, sees her brother's lips move, and knows without needing to be told that he is explaining it all, the cairn and the stones and the bells, one thing at a time.

When he straightens he is smiling.

He says it's a good custom, says Pebble. He says nobody should be buried without someone saying thank you.

They go down the hill together to the road.

Temur walks them to the edge of the village. He does not weep this time; he has done that. He stands in the road with his slate on his chest and his white braid blowing and holds Jian's two hands in his big brown ones, and says something short and fierce that Yue cannot catch.

Then he lets go, and turns, and shouts.

Five riders come out of the tents. They are young men and women, lean and bright-eyed, on small shaggy ponies, each with a bow across the saddle and a leather bag slung at the hip. They draw up in a line, and Temur nods.

"They go south," he says to Jian. "To your Garden. They will ride day and night. Ten days, perhaps nine. They carry word of what we have seen." He smiles, crookedly. "I think the Head of the Sect will wish to know about the grass."

"Thank you."

"It is nothing." He reaches into his cloak and takes out a second slate, small and worn, with a hole bored in the top and a leather cord through it. "This was mine, as a boy. I want you to have it. When you get where you are going, if there is a child there who has not learned his letters..."

Jian takes it. He holds it in both hands, the cord trailing, and his face does a thing that Yue has seen only once before, on the night he flowered his Core.

"I will teach him," he says.

"I know." Temur's grin is wide and wet. "You always did."

The riders wheel. Hooves drum on the frozen road. They are gone in a minute, a streak of dust and a faint rhythm in the soil, heading south, and Yue stands watching them out of sight, and feels in the shifting note of the silver line a small bright thread of hope.

Well, says Pebble. That's the Garden warned.

She nods. She settles her pack. And she turns to look north, where the Sky Wall rises blue-white and enormous, and she realizes that for the first time she can see the door.

It is a notch. A small dark cleft in the cliffs, no more than a mile wide, a long way up. The silver road runs straight toward it across the plain. And as she watches, a thin white plume of what might be snow, or might be breath, lifts slowly out of the notch and drifts away on the wind.

Under her feet the earth gives a single, slow, patient knock.

Who, she signs, to no one, with her hands. What is in there?
